one_liner: Memory-mapped copy-on-write B+tree key-value store in C; 4.6-8.8x faster reads than RocksDB in redb's harness.
what_it_does: LMDB (Lightning Memory-Mapped Database, from OpenLDAP and Symas) is an embedded, fully ACID, ordered key-value library with a simplified BerkeleyDB-style C API. You open an MDB_env on a directory (a data.mdb file plus a lock file), begin a read or write MDB_txn, open one or more named sub-databases (MDB_dbi), and use mdb_get/mdb_put/mdb_del or cursors for ordered range scans; sorted duplicates (MDB_DUPSORT), integer keys and sorted bulk append (MDB_APPEND) are supported. Many threads and processes can share one environment. It is not a drop-in for RocksDB (no compression, column families, merge operators or LSM tuning) or SQLite (no SQL), so callers must be written against its own API or a binding such as Rust's heed.
how_it_is_fast: The whole data file is mapped read-only into memory, and reads walk the B+tree in the map and return pointers into it, so a lookup does no malloc, memcpy or user-space cache lookup (the header: 'no malloc's or memcpy's occur during data fetches'); the OS page cache is the only cache. Concurrency is MVCC by shadow paging: a writer copies the touched leaf-to-root path and commits by updating one of two alternating meta pages, while readers only record their snapshot txnid in a cache-line-padded slot of a shared reader table and take no locks, which is why its lead over RocksDB grows with reader threads (4.8x at 4 threads, 8.8x at 32). Pages freed by old versions are tracked in an internal free-list database and reused once no reader can see them, so there is no write-ahead log, checkpointing or compaction work. The price is a single serialized writer and whole-page copy-on-write for every random update.
when_to_use: Read-dominated workloads whose data or hot set fits in RAM: in redb's harness (5.1M random 24-byte keys with 150-byte values, about a 2.6 GiB LMDB file) LMDB did 1M random point reads in 637 ms vs RocksDB's 2911 ms and 500k ten-element range scans in 565 ms vs 2734 ms.
Many concurrent reader threads or processes on one database: lock-free readers did 5.1M lookups in 125 ms with 32 threads, about 40.8M lookups/s vs about 4.6M/s for RocksDB (derived from page data).

Embedded metadata, configuration, index or directory stores that need ACID commits with no recovery step, background threads or tuning knobs; with default sync settings a single-put durable commit cost about 1.6 ms vs 2.4 ms for RocksDB with sync=true on an NVMe drive.
Code that benefits from zero-copy values (pointers into the map, valid until the transaction ends), or bulk loads of pre-sorted keys with MDB_APPEND, which skips key comparisons.
C or C++ projects that want a small, permissively licensed dependency: two C files (mdb.c, midl.c) and one header, callable from C++ through extern "C".
when_not_to_use: Write-heavy random workloads with batched commits: 100 commits of 1,000 random puts took 942 ms vs 451 ms for RocksDB (2.1x slower) and 353 ms for fjall, and deleting 2.55M keys took 10435 ms vs 6900 ms, because every random update copies whole 4 KiB pages up to the root.

Disk-space or SSD-wear sensitive deployments: there is no compression and the file never shrinks; the same table shows 2.61 GiB vs 893 MiB for RocksDB before compaction and 1.26 GiB vs 455 MiB after, and compaction is only available as a copy to a new file (mdb_env_copy2 with MDB_CP_COMPACT).
Multiple concurrent writers (one write transaction at a time per environment, across all processes) or long-lived read transactions, which pin freed pages and make the file grow quickly.

Data sets far larger than RAM or random reads on slow storage: the cited benchmark is fully memory-resident, and beyond RAM every miss is a synchronous page fault; the header suggests MDB_NORDAHEAD for that case and it is not implemented on Windows.
Network or remote filesystems (explicitly unsupported in lmdb.h), or applications that cannot choose a maximum database size up front.

integration.form: source-drop (mdb.c, midl.c, lmdb.h); the Makefile also builds liblmdb.a and liblmdb.so
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C library, mmap and pthreads
integration.min_toolchain: Any C compiler with pthreads (Makefile default: gcc -pthread -O2 -g); a minimum C standard is not documented
integration.platforms: Linux, BSDs, macOS, Windows and Android; 0.9.34 added NetBSD and Haiku. Needs mmap and working file locks, so not on network filesystems. LMDB 0.9 and 1.0 on-disk formats are mutually incompatible.
integration.thread_safety: An environment can be shared by threads and processes. A transaction and its cursors belong to one thread, and a thread may hold one transaction at a time (MDB_NOTLS lifts this for read-only transactions). Writes are serialized env-wide; readers never block writers or each other. Do not open the same environment twice in one process or use it after fork().

gotchas: Harness asymmetries in the cited redb table (commit d6773ef; the code is unchanged in the current crates/redb-bench-compare): the RocksDB adapter splits the 5M-key bulk load and the 2.55M-key removal into transactions of about 100,000 operations (the ROCKSDB_MAX_WRITES_PER_TXN 'awful hack'), and every chunk after the first is committed through db.transaction(), which uses default WriteOptions and therefore does not sync. RocksDB's removal win (6900 vs 10435 ms) and its bulk-load time are therefore neither atomic nor durable, while LMDB's are single fsynced transactions. In the other direction, RocksDB reads return a heap-allocated Vec copy (snapshot.get) and range iterators return boxed key and value copies, whereas LMDB returns pointers into the map and the harness touches only the first byte, which slightly favours zero-copy engines. The OS, rustc version and C compiler are not stated.

The benchmarked LMDB is not a release: heed 0.22 bundles lmdb-master-sys 0.2.5, which builds the mdb.master development branch at commit f20e41d (version string 0.9.70) with NDEBUG and MDB_IDL_LOGN=16. LMDB 1.0.0 (2026-06-30) and 1.0.1 (2026-08-06) changed the on-disk format (page headers now carry txn IDs; optional page checksums and encryption; page sizes up to 64 KB) and cannot open 0.9 files, so migrating needs mdb_dump with 0.9 and mdb_load with 1.0. LMDB 1.0's performance has not been measured by this harness. A FreeBSD ports search snippet (page blocked here, snippet only) says some applications compiled against 1.0 headers failed silently at run time.

The map size is the hard maximum database size, and the compiled default is only 1 MiB (mdb.c DEFAULT_MAPSIZE; the header comment says 10 MiB). Writes fail with MDB_MAP_FULL when it is exceeded, and it can only be raised with mdb_env_set_mapsize while the process has no active transactions. The harness used 4 GiB for a 2.61 GiB file. Keys are limited to 511 bytes in 0.9 builds, and in 1.0 the limit depends on the page size.

Durability and maintenance traps: MDB_NOSYNC and MDB_WRITEMAP trade crash safety or corruption protection for speed. On macOS older versions did not fully sync commits: redb's harness fsyncs every file after each LMDB commit on macOS, and upstream fixed fdatasync (ITS#10296, 0.9.34) and metapage sync (ITS#10454, 0.9.36) there. Reader slots left by crashed processes block page reuse until mdb_reader_check runs. The GitHub repository is a read-only mirror; bugs go to the OpenLDAP ITS.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LMDB over the RocksDB-family siblings (Badger, Pebble, Speedb, ToplingDB) when reads dominate, the working set fits in RAM, many threads or processes read at once, and you want zero tuning; pick those LSM engines when writes, deletes or disk footprint dominate. UnisonDB claims about 3x LMDB's SET throughput (tier C), and the catalogue also lists libmdbx (an LMDB fork claiming 10-30% gains, first-party) and redb (pure Rust, faster than LMDB on single durable commits but slower on every read row of the same table).
verified_claims_summary: redb's author ran his public Rust harness (commit d6773ef, 2025-08-08; LMDB driven through heed 0.22) on a Ryzen 9950X3D with a Samsung 9100 PRO NVMe drive, with the OS and compilers unstated, on 5.1M random 24/150-byte pairs held in RAM. LMDB was 4.6x faster than RocksDB 0.22 (LZ4, 4 GiB block cache, bloom filters, snapshot reads) on random point reads, 4.8x faster on range scans, 4.8-8.8x faster with 4 to 32 reader threads, and 1.5x faster on bulk load and on single-put synced commits, but 2.1x slower on 1,000-put batch commits, 1.5x slower on bulk removals, and its file was 3x larger. The SQLite ratios in the same table (up to 212x) come from an adapter that re-prepared every statement and ran SQLite untuned, so they should not be used.
status_note: Actively maintained: mdb.master3 had commits on 2026-08-19, and 0.9.36 and 1.0.1 were released on 2026-08-06. The OpenLDAP Public License 2.8 is permissive and the library is two C files, so it is easy to vendor, but choose the 0.9 (mdb.RE/0.9) or 1.0 (mdb.RE/1.0) line deliberately because their file formats are incompatible.
